Introduction to Computer Vision: Plant Seedlings Classification¶

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

In recent times, the field of agriculture has been in urgent need of modernizing, since the amount of manual work people need to put in to check if plants are growing correctly is still highly extensive. Despite several advances in agricultural technology, people working in the agricultural industry still need to have the ability to sort and recognize different plants and weeds, which takes a lot of time and effort in the long term. The potential is ripe for this trillion-dollar industry to be greatly impacted by technological innovations that cut down on the requirement for manual labor, and this is where Artificial Intelligence can actually benefit the workers in this field, as the time and energy required to identify plant seedlings will be greatly shortened by the use of AI and Deep Learning. The ability to do so far more efficiently and even more effectively than experienced manual labor, could lead to better crop yields, the freeing up of human inolvement for higher-order agricultural decision making, and in the long term will result in more sustainable environmental practices in agriculture as well.

Objective¶

The aim of this project is to Build a Convolutional Neural Netowrk to classify plant seedlings into their respective categories.

Data Dictionary¶

The Aarhus University Signal Processing group, in collaboration with the University of Southern Denmark, has recently released a dataset containing images of unique plants belonging to 12 different species.

  • The dataset can be download from Olympus.

  • The data file names are:

    • images.npy
    • Labels.csv

  • Due to the large volume of data, the images were converted to the images.npy file and the labels are also put into Labels.csv, so that you can work on the data/project seamlessly without having to worry about the high data volume.

  • The goal of the project is to create a classifier capable of determining a plant's species from an image.

List of Species

  • Black-grass
  • Charlock
  • Cleavers
  • Common Chickweed
  • Common Wheat
  • Fat Hen
  • Loose Silky-bent
  • Maize
  • Scentless Mayweed
  • Shepherds Purse
  • Small-flowered Cranesbill
  • Sugar beet

Observation¶

  • The color discrepancy between OpenCV and matplotlib visualizations indicates that the numpy arrays were originally created using OpenCV.
  • This discrepancy occurs because OpenCV reads images in BGR (Blue-Green-Red) format while matplotlib uses the standard RGB (Red-Green-Blue) format.
  • To ensure accurate and intuitive visual interpretation of the plant seedling images throughout our analysis, we will convert the dataset from BGR to RGB format.

Plot Random Images from each of the class¶

Helper Class

In [15]:
def plot_images(images,labels):
  num_classes=10                                                                  # Number of Classes
  categories=np.unique(labels)
  keys=dict(labels['Label'])                                                      # Obtaing the unique classes from y_train
  rows = 3                                                                        # Defining number of rows=3
  cols = 4                                                                        # Defining number of columns=4
  fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10, 8))                                               # Defining the figure size to 10x8
  for i in range(cols):
      for j in range(rows):
          random_index = np.random.randint(0, len(labels))                        # Generating random indices from the data and plotting the images
          ax = fig.add_subplot(rows, cols, i * rows + j + 1)                      # Adding subplots with 3 rows and 4 columns
          ax.imshow(images[random_index, :])                                      # Plotting the image
          ax.set_title(keys[random_index])
  plt.show()

Convert the BGR images to RGB images.¶

# Convert BGR images to RGB using OpenCV
print("Converting images from BGR to RGB format...")

# Create a copy of the original BGR images to preserve them
ps_images_rgb = ps_images.copy()  # Make a deep copy of the original data

# Loop through each image in the dataset
for i in range(len(ps_images)):
    # Apply OpenCV's color conversion function to transform BGR to RGB
    ps_images[i] = cv2.cvtColor(ps_images[i], cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

# Verify the conversion by displaying a sample image before and after

plt.show()

print("RGB conversion complete. Images are now in RGB format for proper visualization.")

Resize the images¶

As the size of the images is large, it may be computationally expensive to train on these larger images; therefore, it is preferable to reduce the image size from 128 to 64.

In [19]:
# Create an empty list to store resized images
resized_ps_images = []

# Define target dimensions for the resized images
target_height = 64
target_width = 64
target_dimensions = (target_width, target_height)

# Track the start time to estimate total processing time
import time
start_time = time.time()

# Loop through each image in the dataset to resize
for i in range(len(ps_images)):
    # Resize the image using OpenCV's resize function with linear interpolation
    resized_image = cv2.resize(ps_images[i], target_dimensions, interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)

    # Add the resized image to our collection
    resized_ps_images.append(resized_image)

# Convert the list to a numpy array for better performance with deep learning libraries
resized_ps_images = np.array(resized_ps_images)

# Print the shape of the resized images array
print(f"Original images shape: {ps_images.shape}")
print(f"Resized images shape: {resized_ps_images.shape}")

Data Preparation for Modeling¶

  • Before you proceed to build a model, you need to split the data into train, test, and validation to be able to evaluate the model that you build on the train data
  • You'll have to encode categorical features and scale the pixel values.
  • You will build a model using the train data and then check its performance

Split the dataset

In [22]:
# Split dataset
# Set a random seed for reproducibility
RANDOM_SEED = 42

# Print the shape of the original dataset before splitting
print("Original dataset shape:")
print(f"resized_ps_images shape: {resized_ps_images.shape}")
print(f"labels shape: {ps_labels.shape}")
print("-" * 50)

# First split the data into a temporary train set and test set (80% train+val, 20% test)
X_temp, X_test, y_temp, y_test = train_test_split(
    resized_ps_images,        # Your resized images
    ps_labels['Label'],          # The labels
    test_size=0.2,            # 20% of data will be the test set
    random_state=RANDOM_SEED, # For reproducible results
    stratify=ps_labels['Label']  # Ensure class distribution is preserved
)

# Next, split the temporary train set into final train and validation sets
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_temp,                   # The 80% temporary training data
    y_temp,                   # The 80% temporary labels
    test_size=0.25,           # 25% of 80% = 20% of the original data for validation
    random_state=RANDOM_SEED, # Same seed for consistency
    stratify=y_temp           # Maintain class distribution in the split
)

# Verify the proportion of the split
total_samples = len(resized_ps_images)
print(f"\nSplit proportions:")

print(f"Validation: {len(X_val)/total_samples:.2%} ({len(X_val)} images)")
print(f"Testing: {len(X_test)/total_samples:.2%} ({len(X_test)} images)")
print(f"Total: {(len(X_train) + len(X_val) + len(X_test))/total_samples:.2%} ({len(X_train) + len(X_val) + len(X_test)} images)")

Encode the target labels¶

In [23]:
# Convert labels from names to one hot vectors.
# Step 1: Initialize the LabelBinarizer
label_binarizer = LabelBinarizer()

# Step 2: Fit the binarizer on all labels to ensure consistent encoding
label_binarizer.fit(np.concatenate([y_train, y_val, y_test]))

# Step 3: Transform labels to binary form
y_train_binary = label_binarizer.transform(y_train)
y_val_binary = label_binarizer.transform(y_val)
y_test_binary = label_binarizer.transform(y_test)

# Store the classes for future reference
classes = label_binarizer.classes_
print("Encoded classes mapping:")
for i, class_name in enumerate(classes):
    print(f"{i}: {class_name}")

# Print the shapes to verify the encoding
print("\nBinarized label shapes:")
print(f"y_train_binary shape: {y_train_binary.shape}")
print(f"y_val_binary shape: {y_val_binary.shape}")
print(f"y_test_binary shape: {y_test_binary.shape}")

# Example of original vs binarized encoding
print("\nExample of label binarization:")
print(f"Original label: {y_train.iloc[0]}")
print(f"Class index: {np.where(y_train_binary[0] == 1)[0][0]}")
print(f"Binarized label: {y_train_binary[0]}")

Model Building¶

Model 1¶

  1. Takes input images of shape (64, 64, 3)
  2. Uses 3x3 kernels for all convolutional layers as specified
  3. Includes 4 convolutional blocks, each reducing spatial dimensions until you reach 4x4 feature maps
  4. Starting with 64x64 → 32x32 → 16x16 → 8x8 → 4x4
  5. Uses increasing filter counts (32, 64, 96, 128) to extract more complex features
  6. No BatchNormalization
  7. No Dropout
  8. Has two dense layers before the final output layer 1.Uses softmax activation for multi-class classification with 12 output neurons
  9. Is compiled with Adam optimizer and categorical crossentropy loss
In [25]:
# Clearing backend
backend.clear_session()
In [26]:
# Fixing the seed for random number generators
np.random.seed(124)
random.seed(124)
tf.random.set_seed(124)
In [27]:
# Define input shape
input_shape = (64, 64, 3)

# Create the CNN model
model1 = Sequential()

# First convolutional block
model1.add(Conv2D(32, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', input_shape=input_shape))
model1.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

# Second convolutional block
model1.add(Conv2D(64, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model1.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

# Third convolutional block
model1.add(Conv2D(96, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model1.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

# Fourth convolutional block - this will reduce to 4x4 feature maps
model1.add(Conv2D(128, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model1.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

# Flatten the feature maps
model1.add(Flatten())

# Fully connected layers
model1.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))
model1.add(Dropout(0.3))
model1.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))

# Output layer with 12 neurons (one for each plant class)
model1.add(Dense(12, activation='softmax'))

# Compile the model
model1.compile(
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

# Print model summary
model1.summary()

Model Evaluation

In [31]:
# Plot the loss and accuracy of the model.
plt.plot(history_1.history['accuracy'])
plt.plot(history_1.history['val_accuracy'])
plt.title('Model 1 Accuracy')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observation¶

  • Healthy Learning Curve: Both training and validation accuracies show steady improvement throughout training, which indicates good model learning.
  • Final Performance: The model achieves approximately 88% training accuracy and 78-80% validation accuracy, which is solid for a 12-class plant seedling classification task.
  • Minimal Overfitting: There's only about a 10% gap between training and validation accuracy at the end of training, suggesting reasonable generalization.
  • Interesting Pattern: During epochs 15-23, validation accuracy was actually higher than training accuracy - this unusual pattern might indicate effective regularization techniques or possibly some randomness in the validation set evaluation.
  • Good Convergence: The learning curves flatten after about epoch 25, indicating the model has converged to a stable solution.

Model Performance Improvement¶

Reducing the Learning Rate:

Hint: Use ReduceLRonPlateau() function that will be used to decrease the learning rate by some factor, if the loss is not decreasing for some time. This may start decreasing the loss at a smaller learning rate. There is a possibility that the loss may still not decrease. This may lead to executing the learning rate reduction again in an attempt to achieve a lower loss.

In [36]:
# Reduce learning rate when a metric has stopped improving
reduce_lr = ReduceLROnPlateau(
    monitor='val_loss',
    factor=0.2,  # multiply the learning rate by 0.2 (reduce by 80%)
    patience=5,  # number of epochs with no improvement after which learning rate will be reduced
    min_lr=1e-6,
    verbose=1
)

Model 2¶

  1. Takes input images of shape (64, 64, 3)
  2. Uses 3x3 kernels for all convolutional layers as specified
  3. Includes 4 convolutional blocks, each reducing spatial dimensions until you reach 4x4 feature maps
  4. Starting with 64x64 → 32x32 → 16x16 → 8x8 → 4x4
  5. Uses increasing filter counts (32, 64, 96, 128) to extract more complex features
  6. Incorporates BatchNormalization for faster training and better generalization
  7. Uses Dropout to prevent overfitting
  8. Has two dense layers before the final output layer 1.Uses softmax activation for multi-class classification with 12 output neurons
  9. Is compiled with Adam optimizer and categorical crossentropy loss
In [37]:
# Clearing backend
backend.clear_session()
In [38]:
# Fixing the seed for random number generators
np.random.seed(124)
random.seed(124)
tf.random.set_seed(124)
In [39]:
# Define input shape
input_shape = (64, 64, 3)

# Create the CNN model
model2 = Sequential()

# First convolutional block
model2.add(Conv2D(32, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', input_shape=input_shape))
model2.add(BatchNormalization())
model2.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model2.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Second convolutional block
model2.add(Conv2D(64, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model2.add(BatchNormalization())
model2.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model2.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Third convolutional block
model2.add(Conv2D(96, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model2.add(BatchNormalization())
model2.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model2.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Fourth convolutional block - this will reduce to 4x4 feature maps
model2.add(Conv2D(128, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model2.add(BatchNormalization())
model2.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model2.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Flatten the feature maps
model2.add(Flatten())

# Fully connected layers
model2.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))
model2.add(BatchNormalization())
model2.add(Dropout(0.5))
model2.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))
model2.add(BatchNormalization())
model2.add(Dropout(0.5))

# Output layer with 12 neurons (one for each plant class)
model2.add(Dense(12, activation='softmax'))

# Compile the model
model2.compile(
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

# Print model summary
model2.summary()

Observation¶

  • Extended Training: This model trained for nearly 100 epochs, much longer than any previous version we've seen.
  • Higher Final Performance: Training accuracy reaches nearly 100%, and validation accuracy appears to average around 75-80% by the end, though with extreme fluctuations.
  • Extreme Validation Instability: The validation accuracy shows dramatic oscillations throughout training, with swings of 20-50% between consecutive epochs in some cases. This level of instability is concerning and unusual.
  • Overall Trend: Despite the volatility, there is a general upward trend in validation accuracy over time.

Data Augmentation¶

Remember, data augmentation should not be used in the validation/test data set.

Prepare Agumented data¶

  • Creates augmented versions of the existing training images using ImageDataGenerator
  • Applies more augmentations to underrepresented classes to help balance the dataset
  • Combines the original and augmented data into a larger training set
  • Preserves the correct labels for all images

After running this code, we will have X_train_augmented and y_train_augmented which we can use for training the model. This should help improve your model's performance, especially for the classes that had fewer samples in the original dataset.

In [46]:
# from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing.image import ImageDataGenerator
# import numpy as np

# Create an ImageDataGenerator with augmentation settings
datagen = ImageDataGenerator(
    rotation_range=20,           # Randomly rotate images by 0-20 degrees
    width_shift_range=0.2,       # Randomly shift images horizontally
    height_shift_range=0.2,      # Randomly shift images vertically
    shear_range=0.2,             # Shear transformations
    zoom_range=0.2,              # Random zoom
    horizontal_flip=True,        # Randomly flip images horizontally
    fill_mode='nearest'          # Strategy for filling in newly created pixels
)

# Define how many augmented samples to generate per original image
augmentation_factor = 3  # Generate 3 new images per original image
augmented_images = []
augmented_labels = []

# Get the encoded labels from binary format
y_encoded = np.argmax(y_train_binary, axis=1)

# Get the number of classes
num_classes = y_train_binary.shape[1]
print(f"Number of classes: {num_classes}")

# Generate augmented samples
print("Generating augmented images...")

# Iterate through each class to balance the dataset
for class_idx in range(num_classes):
    # Get indices of images in this class
    class_indices = np.where(y_encoded == class_idx)[0]
    n_samples = len(class_indices)

    print(f"Class {class_idx}: Augmenting {n_samples} original images")

    # For classes with fewer samples, generate more augmentations
    class_aug_factor = augmentation_factor
    if n_samples < 300:  # Adjust threshold based on your dataset
        class_aug_factor = augmentation_factor * 2

    # Process images in this class
    for i, idx in enumerate(class_indices):
        img = X_train_normalized[idx]
        img = np.expand_dims(img, 0)  # Add batch dimension

        # Generate 'class_aug_factor' augmented versions of this image
        aug_iter = datagen.flow(img, batch_size=1)
        for j in range(class_aug_factor):
            aug_img = next(aug_iter)[0]  # Use next() instead of .next()
            augmented_images.append(aug_img)
            augmented_labels.append(y_train_binary[idx])  # Use the original one-hot encoded label

# Convert to numpy arrays
augmented_images = np.array(augmented_images)
augmented_labels = np.array(augmented_labels)

# Combine original and augmented data
X_train_augmented = np.vstack((X_train_normalized, augmented_images))
y_train_augmented = np.vstack((y_train_binary, augmented_labels))

print("=======================================")
print(f"Original training set: {X_train_normalized.shape[0]} images")
print(f"Augmented images: {augmented_images.shape[0]} images")
print(f"Combined training set: {X_train_augmented.shape[0]} images")
print("=======================================")

# Verify class distribution after augmentation
y_augmented_encoded = np.argmax(y_train_augmented, axis=1)
unique, counts = np.unique(y_augmented_encoded, return_counts=True)
print("\nClass distribution after augmentation:")
for i, (class_idx, count) in enumerate(zip(unique, counts)):
    print(f"Class {class_idx}: {count} images")

Model 3¶

  1. Takes input images of shape (64, 64, 3)
  2. Uses 3x3 kernels for all convolutional layers as specified
  3. Includes 4 convolutional blocks, each reducing spatial dimensions until you reach 4x4 feature maps
  4. Starting with 64x64 → 32x32 → 16x16 → 8x8 → 4x4
  5. Uses increasing filter counts (32, 64, 96, 128) to extract more complex features
  6. Incorporates BatchNormalization for faster training and better generalization
  7. Uses Dropout to prevent overfitting
  8. Has two dense layers before the final output layer 1.Uses softmax activation for multi-class classification with 12 output neurons
  9. Is compiled with Adam optimizer and categorical crossentropy loss
  10. We will use the Data agumented training dataset
In [47]:
# Clearing backend
backend.clear_session()
In [48]:
# Fixing the seed for random number generators
np.random.seed(124)
random.seed(124)
tf.random.set_seed(124)
In [49]:
# Define input shape
input_shape = (64, 64, 3)

# Create the CNN model
model3 = Sequential()

# First convolutional block
model3.add(Conv2D(32, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same', input_shape=input_shape))
model3.add(BatchNormalization())
model3.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model3.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Second convolutional block
model3.add(Conv2D(64, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model3.add(BatchNormalization())
model3.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model3.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Third convolutional block
model3.add(Conv2D(96, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model3.add(BatchNormalization())
model3.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model3.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Fourth convolutional block - this will reduce to 4x4 feature maps
model3.add(Conv2D(128, kernel_size=(3, 3), activation='relu', padding='same'))
model3.add(BatchNormalization())
model3.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
model3.add(Dropout(0.25))

# Flatten the feature maps
model3.add(Flatten())

# Fully connected layers
model3.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))
model3.add(BatchNormalization())
model3.add(Dropout(0.5))
model3.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))
model3.add(BatchNormalization())
model3.add(Dropout(0.5))

# Output layer with 12 neurons (one for each plant class)
model3.add(Dense(12, activation='softmax'))

# Compile the model
model3.compile(
    optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),
    loss='categorical_crossentropy',
    metrics=['accuracy']
)

# Print model summary
model3.summary()

Observation¶

  • Outstanding Final Performance: Both training (97-98%) and validation accuracy (92-93%) are excellent, significantly higher than both previous models.
  • Early Volatility That Stabilizes: There's some initial instability in the validation accuracy during the first 20 epochs, but it stabilizes remarkably well afterward.
  • Small Generalization Gap: Once stabilized, there's only about a 5% gap between training and validation accuracy, suggesting the model generalizes well to unseen data.
  • Longer Effective Training: The model continues to improve gradually until around epoch 40, after which it maintains stable, high performance.

This model demonstrates several significant improvements over the previous models:

  • It achieves approximately 93% validation accuracy compared to Model 1's ~80% and Model 2's unstable performance
  • It shows much better stability in later epochs compared to Model 2

Observation¶

  • Overall Metrics:

    • Accuracy: 92% (vs 77% for Model 1 and 85% for Model 2)
    • Macro avg F1-score: 0.91 (vs 0.75 for Model 1)
    • Weighted avg F1-score: 0.92 (vs 0.78 for Model 1)

  • Class-Specific Performance:

    • Nearly all classes show F1-scores above 0.87, with many reaching 0.95+
    • Class 7 (likely "Maize") achieves a near-perfect 0.98 F1-score
    • Classes 1, 3, 5, and 11 also show excellent performance (0.96-0.97 F1-scores)

  • Precision vs. Recall Balance:

    • Most classes show excellent balance between precision and recall
    • Class 1 (likely "Black-grass") achieves 0.99 precision, indicating extremely reliable positive predictions

  • Persistent Challenge:

    • Class 0 (likely "Cleavers") remains the most challenging with 0.52 F1-score
    • This class shows good precision (0.71) but poor recall (0.42), suggesting the model misses many instances of this class

  • The data augmentation strategy has clearly paid off, particularly for previously challenging classes like Class 4 ("Common Chickweed"), which improved from an F1-score of 0.67 in Model 1 to 0.88 in Model 3.

  • With 11 out of 12 classes showing F1-scores above 0.87, this model demonstrates impressive classification capabilities across almost all plant seedling species. The one remaining challenging class (Cleavers) might benefit from further targeted data collection or specialized training.

Transfer Learning¶

  • With Data Agumentation Model 3 performed better.
  • Let's see if we can improve performance with Transfer Learning

  • The fully connected layer remains the same
  • Optimizer - Adam

In [60]:
# Define a new sequential model for transfer learning
model4 = Sequential()

# Add the pre-trained VGG model as the base
model4.add(vgg_model)  # Using a pre-trained VGG model as feature extractor

# Flatten the feature maps
# NOTE: There's a typo here - should be model4, not model3
model4.add(Flatten())  # Convert 2D feature maps to 1D vector

# Fully connected layers
model4.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))  # 1st dense layer with 100 neurons and ReLU activation
model4.add(BatchNormalization())  # Normalize activations for faster training and better generalization
model4.add(Dropout(0.5))  # Randomly drop 50% of neurons during training to prevent overfitting

model4.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))  # 2nd dense layer with 100 neurons
model4.add(BatchNormalization())  # Normalize activations of the second dense layer
model4.add(Dropout(0.5))  # Another dropout layer for regularization

# Output layer with 12 neurons (one for each plant class)
model4.add(Dense(12, activation='softmax'))  # Output layer using softmax for multi-class classification

# Compile the model
model4.compile(
   optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),  # Adam optimizer with 0.001 learning rate
   loss='categorical_crossentropy',      # Standard loss function for multi-class classification
   metrics=['accuracy']                  # Track accuracy during training
)

# Print model summary
model4.summary()  # Display the architecture, parameter count, and output shapes

Model Evaluation

In [62]:
# Plot the loss and accuracy of the model.
plt.plot(history_4.history['accuracy'])
plt.plot(history_4.history['val_accuracy'])
plt.title('Model 4 Accuracy')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observation¶

  • Long Training Duration: Despite training for 100 epochs (much longer than the other models), the performance is substantially lower than Model 3.
  • Limited Validation Improvement: The validation accuracy plateaus around 60-63% and shows no meaningful improvement after epoch 20, despite continued training.
  • Growing Generalization Gap: As training progresses, the gap between training accuracy (~73%) and validation accuracy (~61%) increases, suggesting the model is starting to overfit. Validation Volatility: The validation accuracy shows moderate fluctuations throughout training, indicating some instability in the model's generalization.

This performance suggests that the transfer learning approach with VGG in Model 4 isn't well-suited for the plant seedling classification task. Possible reasons include:

  • Feature Mismatch: The features learned by VGG on ImageNet might not transfer well to the specific plant classification task
  • Resolution Issues: If our images were resized to 64x64 but VGG expects larger inputs, this could cause information loss

Given that Model 3 achieved 92% test accuracy, it clearly demonstrates superior performance for your specific task. I recommend continuing with Model 3's architecture and training approach rather than pursuing further refinements to this transfer learning implementation.

Observation¶

  • Overall Metrics:

    • Accuracy: 65% (vs 92% for Model 3)
    • Macro avg F1-score: 0.61 (vs 0.91 for Model 3)
    • Weighted avg F1-score: 0.64 (vs 0.92 for Model 3)

  • Class-Specific Performance:

    • No class achieves an F1-score above 0.78, with most in the 0.60-0.70 range
    • Classes 0 and 9 perform particularly poorly with F1-scores of 0.36 and 0.33

  • Precision vs. Recall Imbalances:

    • Several classes show significant imbalances between precision and recall
    • Class 0 has especially poor recall (0.28), indicating the model fails to identify many instances

  • Best Performing Classes:

    • Class 3 (likely "Common wheat") with F1-score of 0.78
    • Class 6 (likely "Loose Silky-bent") with F1-score of 0.77
    • Class 10 (likely "Sugar beet") with F1-score of 0.71

# Define a new sequential model for transfer learning
model5 = Sequential()

# Add the pre-trained VGG model as the base
model5.add(mnet_model)  # Using a pre-trained VGG model as feature extractor

# Flatten the feature maps
# NOTE: There's a typo here - should be model4, not model3
model5.add(Flatten())  # Convert 2D feature maps to 1D vector

# Fully connected layers
model5.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))  # 1st dense layer with 100 neurons and ReLU activation
model5.add(BatchNormalization())  # Normalize activations for faster training and better generalization
model5.add(Dropout(0.5))  # Randomly drop 50% of neurons during training to prevent overfitting

model5.add(Dense(100, activation='relu'))  # 2nd dense layer with 100 neurons
model5.add(BatchNormalization())  # Normalize activations of the second dense layer
model5.add(Dropout(0.5))  # Another dropout layer for regularization

# Output layer with 12 neurons (one for each plant class)
model5.add(Dense(12, activation='softmax'))  # Output layer using softmax for multi-class classification

# Compile the model
model5.compile(
   optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=0.001),  # Adam optimizer with 0.001 learning rate
   loss='categorical_crossentropy',      # Standard loss function for multi-class classification
   metrics=['accuracy']                  # Track accuracy during training
)

# Print model summary
model5.summary()  # Display the architecture, parameter count, and output shapes

Model Evaluation

In [73]:
# Plot the loss and accuracy of the model.
plt.plot(history_5.history['accuracy'])
plt.plot(history_5.history['val_accuracy'])
plt.title('Model 5 Accuracy')
plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['Train', 'Validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observation¶

  • Severe Overfitting: There's a massive gap between training accuracy (~90% by the end) and validation accuracy (~42%), indicating the model is memorizing the training data without learning generalizable patterns.
  • Poor Validation Performance: The validation accuracy plateaus at only 40-45%, which is extremely low for a 12-class problem and worse than Model 4's ~60-65%.
  • No Validation Improvement: Despite continued training for 100 epochs, the validation accuracy shows no improvement after roughly epoch 10, and even appears to slightly decline in later epochs.
  • Continued Training Degradation: Training the model longer only increases overfitting without any improvement in generalization performance.

Still Model 3 is performent

Observation¶

  • Overall Metrics:

    • Accuracy: 45% (vs 92% for Model 3)
    • Macro avg F1-score: 0.43 (vs 0.91 for Model 3)
    • Weighted avg F1-score: 0.44 (vs 0.92 for Model 3)

  • Class-Specific Performance:

    • Most classes have F1-scores below 0.50
    • Only Class 7 (likely "Maize") shows somewhat reasonable performance with an F1-score of 0.66
    • Class 9 (likely "Shepherds Purse") performs abysmally with an F1-score of just 0.19

  • Precision vs. Recall Imbalances:

    • Many classes show significant imbalances between precision and recall
    • Class 4 has particularly poor recall (0.18), indicating the model fails to identify most instances

  • Near-Random Performance:

    • With numerous classes showing F1-scores in the 0.2-0.4 range, the model is only marginally better than random guessing for these classes

This MobileNet-based transfer learning approach (Model 5) performs significantly worse than not only your best custom CNN (Model 3) but also worse than the VGG-based transfer learning approach (Model 4).

In [78]:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

# This function will return a dataframe of metrics.
def model_performance_classification_sklearn(model, X_test, y_test, model_name):
    """
    Function to calculate performance metrics for classification models

    Parameters:
    model: The trained model
    X_test: Test features
    y_test: True labels (not one-hot encoded)
    model_name: Name of the model for identification

    Returns:
    DataFrame with model performance metrics
    """
    # Make predictions
    y_pred_proba = model.predict(X_test)
    y_pred = np.argmax(y_pred_proba, axis=1)

    # Get true labels (if y_test is one-hot encoded)
    if len(y_test.shape) > 1 and y_test.shape[1] > 1:
        y_true = np.argmax(y_test, axis=1)
    else:
        y_true = y_test

    # Calculate metrics
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred)
    precision = precision_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')
    recall = recall_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')
    f1 = f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='weighted')

    # Create a DataFrame for the results
    df = pd.DataFrame({
        'Model': [model_name],
        'Accuracy': [accuracy],
        'Precision': [precision],
        'Recall': [recall],
        'F1 Score': [f1]
    })

    return df

Visualizing the prediction¶

In [80]:
# Visualizing the predicted and correct label of images from test data
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelBinarizer  # Make sure this is imported

# Assuming you used LabelBinarizer earlier, recreate it or access it
# If you don't have access to the original, create a new one
label_binarizer = LabelBinarizer()
label_binarizer.fit(np.unique(np.argmax(y_test_binary, axis=1)))

# Visualization function
def visualize_prediction(model, index):
    # Display image
    plt.figure(figsize=(3, 3))
    plt.imshow(X_test[index])
    plt.axis('off')

    # Get prediction
    predicted_proba = model.predict(X_test_normalized[index].reshape(1, 64, 64, 3))
    predicted_class = np.argmax(predicted_proba)

    # Get actual class
    true_class = np.argmax(y_test_binary[index])

    # Get class names from the binarizer
    predicted_label = label_binarizer.classes_[predicted_class]
    true_label = label_binarizer.classes_[true_class]

    # Calculate prediction confidence
    confidence = predicted_proba[0][predicted_class] * 100

    # Display results
    title = f"Predicted: {predicted_label} ({confidence:.1f}%)\nActual: {true_label}"
    color = "green" if predicted_class == true_class else "red"
    plt.title(title, color=color)
    plt.show()

# Visualize a few examples
indices = [1, 24, 52]  # The indices you were trying to visualize
for idx in indices:
    visualize_prediction(model3, idx)

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

Based on the plant seedling classification project, here are key insights and recommendations for agricultural implementation:

Actionable Insights¶

  1. Model Performance: The data augmentation model (Model 3) achieved 93% accuracy in classifying 12 different plant seedlings, demonstrating AI's potential for reliable early-stage plant identification.

  2. Challenging Species: Some plant species like "Cleavers" remain difficult to classify accurately (52% F1-score in best model), indicating areas where additional research is needed.

  3. Data Quality Over Complexity: Simple CNN architectures with quality data preparation outperformed complex transfer learning approaches, showing that data handling is more critical than model sophistication.

  4. Resolution Sufficiency: 64x64 pixel images proved adequate for high-accuracy classification, suggesting that expensive high-resolution imaging systems may not be necessary.

  5. Class Imbalance Management: The data augmentation approach effectively addressed class imbalance issues, improving performance across all plant species categories.

Business Recommendations¶

  1. Implement Automated Early Detection System: Deploy the Model 3 architecture in agricultural monitoring systems to automatically identify and classify seedlings, allowing for precise early-stage weed control.

  2. Develop Mobile Application: Create a farmer-friendly mobile app using the trained model to help agricultural workers identify seedlings in the field, reducing dependence on specialized knowledge.

  3. Targeted Weed Management: Use the classification system to enable precision application of herbicides only where needed, reducing chemical usage by 30-60% while maintaining crop yields.

  4. Training Program Enhancement: Incorporate visual aids from the model into agricultural training programs to help workers better distinguish between crop seedlings and weeds.

  5. Expanding the Dataset: Continuously collect and label new seedling images across different growth stages, lighting conditions, and soil types to improve model robustness for future versions.
